Buy and Sell Stock.title: Buy and Sell Stock
Buy and Sell Stock.problemStatement: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the ith day. You want to maximize your profit by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock. Return the maximum profit you can achieve from this transaction. If you cannot achieve any profit, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price = 1) and sell on day 5 (price = 6), profit = 6-1 = 5.
In this case, no transactions are done and the max profit = 0.

edgeCases: Prices are in strictly descending order (profit is 0)
Array size is 1 (cannot buy and sell, profit is 0)
followUps: What if you can buy and sell multiple times (Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II)?
What if you can only complete at most k transactions (Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Check all possible pairs of buy and sell days where the sell day is after the buy day. Find the maximum difference prices[j] - prices[i].
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize max_profit to 0.
2. Run a loop with index i from 0 to N-1 (buy day).
3. Run a nested loop with index j from i+1 to N-1 (sell day).
4. Compute the difference prices[j] - prices[i]. If it is greater than max_profit, update max_profit.
5. Return max_profit.
approaches.code:
def maxProfit(prices):
    # Initialize the maximum profit to 0
    max_profit = 0
    # Loop through the list to pick the buying price
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        # Loop through the remaining days to pick the selling price
        for j in range(i + 1, len(prices)):
            # Calculate potential profit
            profit = prices[j] - prices[i]
            # Update max_profit if current profit is higher
            if profit > max_profit:
                max_profit = profit
    # Return the final maximum profit found
    return max_profit

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: As we iterate through the price list, we keep track of the minimum price observed so far. At each step, we calculate the profit if we sell at the current price and update the maximum profit.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize min_price to infinity and max_profit to 0.
2. Iterate through each price in the prices array.
3. Update min_price if the current price is lower.
4. Calculate the profit (current price - min_price). Update max_profit if it is greater than the current max_profit.
5. Return max_profit.
approaches.code:
def maxProfit(prices):
    # Start min_price as infinity to find the true minimum
    min_price = float('inf')
    # Start max_profit at 0
    max_profit = 0
    # Loop through each price in the input list
    for price in prices:
        # Check if the current price is the lowest seen so far
        if price < min_price:
            min_price = price
        # Check if selling at the current price yields a higher profit
        elif price - min_price > max_profit:
            max_profit = price - min_price
    # Return the maximum profit achieved
    return max_profit

Rotate Matrix.title: Rotate Matrix
Rotate Matrix.problemStatement: You are given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees (clockwise). You have to rotate the image in-place, which means you have to modify the input 2D matrix directly. DO NOT allocate another 2D matrix.
followUps: How would you rotate the matrix anti-clockwise?
Can you perform this rotation in O(1) space without transpose?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use an auxiliary matrix of size n x n. Place the element matrix[i][j] at dummy[j][n - 1 - i]. Then copy dummy back to original matrix.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize a dummy 2D array of size n x n.
2. Iterate through matrix, set dummy[j][n - 1 - i] = matrix[i][j].
3. Copy dummy back to matrix.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: We can rotate the matrix in-place by performing two steps. First, we transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]). Second, we reverse each row of the transposed matrix.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Transpose the matrix: Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for i from 0 to N-1, and j from i+1 to N-1.
2. Reverse each row of the matrix.
3. The matrix is now rotated by 90 degrees clockwise.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
Merge Overlapping Intervals.problemStatement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals.
edgeCases: Only 1 interval in the input list
All intervals completely overlap with each other
Intervals are already sorted and disjoint
followUps: What if the input intervals are already sorted by start time?
How would you merge them if you cannot sort the list first (e.g. interval tree / stream inputs)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Sort intervals first. For each interval, check if it can merge with subsequent intervals. Repeat this process until no overlapping intervals are found.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort the intervals.
2. Repeat: Check if any adjacent intervals overlap. If yes, merge them by updating end time and pop the redundant one.
3. Return the merged list when no more overlaps exist.
approaches.code:
def merge(intervals):
    # Sort the intervals first
    intervals.sort()
    # Flag to track if a merge took place
    merged = True
    # Loop until no more merges can be made
    while merged:
        merged = False
        i = 0
        # Iterate through adjacent intervals
        while i < len(intervals) - 1:
            # Check if current interval overlaps with the next
            if intervals[i][1] >= intervals[i + 1][0]:
                # Merge by updating the end time
                intervals[i][1] = max(intervals[i][1], intervals[i + 1][1])
                # Remove the next interval since it is merged
                intervals.pop(i + 1)
                # Mark that we completed a merge
                merged = True
            else:
                # Increment loop index if no merge occurs
                i += 1
    # Return the merged list
    return intervals

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Sort intervals by start time. Iterate through the intervals, adding the first one to a result list. For subsequent intervals, if the start of current is <= end of the last in result, merge them by updating end. Otherwise, append the current interval.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort intervals by start time.
2. Initialize merged = [].
3. Iterate through intervals. If merged is empty or last element in merged doesn't overlap, append current.
4. Else, update end of last element in merged to max(merged[-1][1], current[1]).
5. Return merged.
approaches.code:
def merge(intervals):
    # Sort intervals by start time
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    # List to store merged intervals
    merged = []
    # Iterate through each interval
    for interval in intervals:
        # If merged is empty or no overlap with last interval
        if not merged or merged[-1][1] < interval[0]:
            # Append the current interval
            merged.append(interval)
        else:
            # Update the end time of the last interval to merge them
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], interval[1])
    # Return the result list
    return merged

Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Space
Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.problemStatement: Given two sorted arrays arr1[] of size n and arr2[] of size m, merge them in-place in sorted order such that arr1[] contains the first n elements and arr2[] contains the remaining m elements. Do not use any extra space.
edgeCases: All elements of arr1 are smaller than arr2
All elements of arr1 are larger than arr2
followUps: Can you solve it in linear time O(N+M) with O(1) extra space?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Combine both arrays into a temporary list, sort it, and then copy the sorted elements back to both arrays.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Create combined = arr1 + arr2.
2. Sort combined.
3. Copy first n elements back to arr1.
4. Copy remaining elements back to arr2.
approaches.code:
def merge(arr1, arr2):
    # Combine both arrays into one
    combined = arr1 + arr2
    # Sort the combined array
    combined.sort()
    # Copy first n elements to arr1
    for i in range(len(arr1)):
        arr1[i] = combined[i]
    # Copy remaining m elements to arr2
    for j in range(len(arr2)):
        arr2[j] = combined[len(arr1) + j]

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Use the Gap Method (Shell Sort variant). The initial gap is ceil((n+m)/2). We compare elements at gap distance and swap if out of order. We then halve the gap and repeat until the gap is 0.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Calculate initial gap = ceil((n + m) / 2).
2. Place left pointer at 0 and right at left + gap.
3. Traverse and swap elements if arr[left] > arr[right]. Handle cases where left and right fall in arr1 or arr2.
4. Reduce gap = ceil(gap / 2) and repeat until gap is 0.
approaches.code:
import math

def merge(arr1, arr2):
    # Get sizes of arrays
    n = len(arr1)
    m = len(arr2)
    # Total size of combined arrays
    total_len = n + m
    # Set initial gap
    gap = math.ceil(total_len / 2)
    # Run gap method
    while gap > 0:
        left = 0
        right = left + gap
        # Traverse elements with gap distance
        while right < total_len:
            # Case 1: left in arr1 and right in arr2
            if left < n and right >= n:
                idx2 = right - n
                if arr1[left] > arr2[idx2]:
                    arr1[left], arr2[idx2] = arr2[idx2], arr1[left]
            # Case 2: both in arr2
            elif left >= n:
                idx1 = left - n
                idx2 = right - n
                if arr2[idx1] > arr2[idx2]:
                    arr2[idx1], arr2[idx2] = arr2[idx2], arr2[idx1]
            # Case 3: both in arr1
            else:
                if arr1[left] > arr1[right]:
                    arr1[left], arr1[right] = arr1[right], arr1[left]
            # Advance pointers
            left += 1
            right += 1
        # Stop if gap was 1
        if gap == 1:
            break
        # Update gap to half
        gap = math.ceil(gap / 2)

trace.desc: left in arr1, right in arr2. Swap since arr1[0] (3) > arr2[0] (1)
left in arr1, right in arr2. Swap since arr1[1] (4) > arr2[1] (2)
Outer iteration done, update gap to ceil(2/2) = 1
Compare inside arr1: arr1[0] (1) and arr1[1] (2). No swap.

Find Duplicate Number.title: Find Duplicate Number
Find Duplicate Number.problemStatement: Given an array of integers nums containing n + 1 integers where each integer is in the range [1, n] inclusive. There is only one repeated number in nums, return this repeated number. Do not modify the array and use constant extra space.
edgeCases: Duplicate number appears more than twice
followUps: Can you solve it in O(N) time and O(1) space if modifying the array is allowed?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use a hash set to keep track of visited numbers. Return the first number that is already in the set.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty set 'seen'.
2. For each number in the array, check if it exists in 'seen'.
3. If yes, return it.
4. Else, add it to 'seen'.
approaches.code:
def findDuplicate(nums):
    # Create a set to record visited numbers
    seen = set()
    # Iterate through numbers
    for num in nums:
        # Check if current number was seen before
        if num in seen:
            return num
        # Add current number to the set
        seen.add(num)
    # Fallback return
    return -1

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare Cycle Detection. We can model the array as a linked list where indices point to values. Since there is a duplicate, a cycle must exist. We use two pointers to find the cycle intersection and then find the start of the cycle.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize tortoise = nums[0], hare = nums[0].
2. In a loop, tortoise = nums[tortoise], hare = nums[nums[hare]] until they meet.
3. Reset tortoise to nums[0].
4. Advance both pointers by 1 step at a time until they meet again.
5. Return the meeting point, which is the start of the cycle (the duplicate).
approaches.code:
def findDuplicate(nums):
    # Phase 1: Detect cycle using slow and fast pointers
    tortoise = nums[0]
    hare = nums[0]
    # Move pointers until they meet
    while True:
        # Tortoise moves 1 step
        tortoise = nums[tortoise]
        # Hare moves 2 steps
        hare = nums[nums[hare]]
        # Check if they intersect
        if tortoise == hare:
            break
    # Phase 2: Find cycle entry point
    tortoise = nums[0]
    # Move both 1 step at a time
    while tortoise != hare:
        tortoise = nums[tortoise]
        hare = nums[hare]
    # Both met at cycle entry point
    return tortoise

trace.desc: Tortoise moves to nums[1] = 3, Hare moves to nums[2] = 2
Tortoise moves to nums[3] = 2, Hare moves to nums[2] = 2

Repeat and Missing Number.title: Repeat and Missing Number
Repeat and Missing Number.problemStatement: You are given a read-only array of n integers from 1 to n. Each integer appears exactly once except A which appears twice and B which is missing. Return A and B.
followUps: Can you solve it using XOR operations without overflow issues?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use a frequency array to record count of each element. The number with count 2 is repeating, and count 0 is missing.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize a count array of size n+1 with 0s.
2. Iterate through input, incrementing counts.
3. Loop from 1 to n to find elements with count 2 and 0.
4. Return them.
approaches.code:
def findRepeatAndMissing(arr):
    # Get array size
    n = len(arr)
    # Count array initialized to zero
    count = [0] * (n + 1)
    # Count frequencies
    for x in arr:
        count[x] += 1
    # Track repeating and missing
    repeat = -1
    missing = -1
    # Check values from 1 to n
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if count[i] == 2:
            repeat = i
        elif count[i] == 0:
            missing = i
    # Return final results
    return [repeat, missing]

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition:
Use mathematical equations based on sums. Sum of 1 to n is S. Sum of squares is P. Sum of elements is S_act. Sum of squares is P_act.
S_act - S = R - M
P_act - P = R^2 - M^2 = (R-M)(R+M)
Solve these to find R and M.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Compute sum_n and sum_n_sq.
2. Compute sum_act and sum_act_sq.
3. diff1 = sum_act - sum_n (R - M).
4. diff2 = sum_act_sq - sum_n_sq (R^2 - M^2).
5. sum_rm = diff2 // diff1 (R + M).
6. R = (diff1 + sum_rm) // 2.
7. M = sum_rm - R.
8. Return [R, M].
approaches.code:
def findRepeatAndMissing(arr):
    # Size of the array
    n = len(arr)
    # Expected sum from 1 to n
    sum_n = (n * (n + 1)) // 2
    # Expected sum of squares from 1 to n
    sum_n_sq = (n * (n + 1) * (2 * n + 1)) // 6
    # Actual sum and sum of squares
    sum_act = sum(arr)
    sum_act_sq = sum(x * x for x in arr)
    # equations: diff1 = R - M
    diff1 = sum_act - sum_n
    # diff2 = R^2 - M^2
    diff2 = sum_act_sq - sum_n_sq
    # sum_rm = R + M
    sum_rm = diff2 // diff1
    # Calculate repeat R
    repeat = (diff1 + sum_rm) // 2
    # Calculate missing M
    missing = sum_rm - repeat
    # Return repeat and missing
    return [repeat, missing]

Inversion Count.title: Inversion Count
Inversion Count.problemStatement: Given an array of integers. Find the Inversion Count in the array. Two array elements arr[i] and arr[j] form an inversion if arr[i] > arr[j] and i < j.
edgeCases: Array is already sorted (inversion count is 0)
Array is sorted in reverse (inversion count is N * (N - 1) / 2)
followUps: Can you solve it in O(N log N) using a Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use nested loops to check all pairs (i, j) where i < j. If arr[i] > arr[j], increment count.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize count = 0.
2. Outer loop i from 0 to N-1.
3. Inner loop j from i+1 to N-1.
4. If arr[i] > arr[j], count += 1.
5. Return count.
approaches.code:
def countInversions(arr):
    # Get size of array
    n = len(arr)
    # Initialize count to 0
    count = 0
    # Loop through all elements
    for i in range(n):
        # Compare with subsequent elements
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            # Check inversion condition
            if arr[i] > arr[j]:
                count += 1
    # Return final inversion count
    return count

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Adapt the Merge Sort algorithm. During the merge step, if we find that arr[i] > arr[j] (where arr[i] is in the left half and arr[j] is in the right half), then all elements from index i to the end of the left half are also greater than arr[j]. We add (mid - i + 1) to our inversion count.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Implement merge sort recursively.
2. In merge function, maintain pointers i, j. If arr[i] <= arr[j], merge arr[i].
3. If arr[i] > arr[j], merge arr[j] and add (mid - i + 1) to count.
4. Return accumulated counts.
approaches.code:
def countInversions(arr):
    # Helper recursive function
    def merge_sort(temp_arr, left, right):
        inv_count = 0
        if left < right:
            mid = (left + right) // 2
            inv_count += merge_sort(temp_arr, left, mid)
            inv_count += merge_sort(temp_arr, mid + 1, right)
            inv_count += merge(temp_arr, left, mid, right)
        return inv_count

    # Merge step that counts cross-inversions
    def merge(temp_arr, left, mid, right):
        i = left
        j = mid + 1
        k = left
        inv_count = 0
        while i <= mid and j <= right:
            if arr[i] <= arr[j]:
                temp_arr[k] = arr[i]
                i += 1
            else:
                temp_arr[k] = arr[j]
                inv_count += (mid - i + 1)
                j += 1
            k += 1
        while i <= mid:
            temp_arr[k] = arr[i]
            i += 1
            k += 1
        while j <= right:
            temp_arr[k] = arr[j]
            j += 1
            k += 1
        for loop_var in range(left, right + 1):
            arr[loop_var] = temp_arr[loop_var]
        return inv_count

    # Initialize temp array
    temp_arr = [0] * len(arr)
    return merge_sort(temp_arr, 0, len(arr) - 1)

trace.desc: Start merge sort with left=0, right=3
Merge step for left=[2, 4] and right=[1, 3]
arr[i] (2) > arr[j] (1). Copy arr[j]. Add (1-0+1) = 2 to inv_count
arr[i] (2) <= arr[j] (3). Copy arr[i]. Increment i.
arr[i] (4) > arr[j] (3). Copy arr[j]. Add (1-1+1) = 1 to inv_count
Copy remaining left subarray arr[i] (4) to temp_arr

Search in a 2D Matrix.title: Search in a 2D Matrix
Search in a 2D Matrix.problemStatement: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a value target in an m x n integer matrix matrix. Integers in each row are sorted from left to right. The first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row.
edgeCases: Target is smaller than the first element or larger than the last element
followUps: How would you solve this if the matrix rows are sorted but columns are also sorted, and first element of a row isn't necessarily larger than the last element of the previous row (Search in 2D Matrix II)?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Linearly scan all elements of the 2D matrix to search for the target.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Loop through each row of the matrix.
2. Loop through each column element of the row.
3. If target matches, return True. If loop completes, return False.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Treat the 2D matrix as a sorted 1D array of size m * n. Run a binary search. A 1D index 'mid' can be mapped to 2D row = mid // cols and col = mid % cols.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize left = 0, right = rows * cols - 1.
2. Compute mid = (left + right) // 2.
3. Map mid to matrix[mid // cols][mid % cols].
4. Perform standard binary search comparison to update left or right.
5. Return True if found, False otherwise.
approaches.code:
def searchMatrix(matrix, target):
    # Check for empty matrix
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]:
        return False
    # Dimensions of matrix
    rows = len(matrix)
    cols = len(matrix[0])
    # Binary search boundaries
    left = 0
    right = rows * cols - 1
    # Start binary search
    while left <= right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        # Map 1D index to 2D index
        mid_val = matrix[mid // cols][mid % cols]
        # Check if mid value is target
        if mid_val == target:
            return True
        # If mid_val is smaller, search right half
        elif mid_val < target:
            left = mid + 1
        # Otherwise search left half
        else:
            right = mid - 1
    # Return False if target not found
    return False

trace.desc: Check condition: left <= right (0 <= 3 is True)
Map mid=1 to row=0, col=1. mid_val = matrix[0][1] = 3
Check condition: left <= right (2 <= 3 is True)
Map mid=2 to row=1, col=0. mid_val = matrix[1][0] = 5
5 == 5 is True. Target found. Return True.

Pow(x, n).title: Pow(x, n)
Pow(x, n).problemStatement: Implement pow(x, n), which calculates x raised to the power n (i.e., x^n).
constraints: Either x is not zero or n > 0
edgeCases: n is the lowest possible negative integer -2^31
followUps: Can you implement this iteratively and recursively?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Multiply x, n times. If n is negative, invert the base x and change n to positive.
approaches.algorithm:
1. If n == 0, return 1.
2. If n < 0, invert base x = 1/x and let n = -n.
3. Multiply result by x, n times.
4. Return result.
approaches.code:
def myPow(x, n):
    # Return 1.0 if exponent is 0
    if n == 0:
        return 1.0
    # Handle negative exponent
    if n < 0:
        x = 1 / x
        n = -n
    ans = 1.0
    # Multiply x, n times
    for _ in range(n):
        ans *= x
    # Return final product
    return ans

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Binary Exponentiation. If n is even, x^n = (x^2)^(n/2). If n is odd, x^n = x * x^(n-1). This reduces calculations to O(log N).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Store original exponent. Work with absolute exponent nn = |n|.
2. Run a loop while nn > 0.
3. If nn is odd, multiply ans by x and reduce nn by 1.
4. If nn is even, square x and divide nn by 2.
5. If n was negative, return 1 / ans. Else return ans.
approaches.code:
def myPow(x, n):
    # Base case
    if n == 0:
        return 1.0
    # Working variable for positive exponent
    nn = n if n >= 0 else -n
    ans = 1.0
    # Binary exponentiation loop
    while nn > 0:
        # If exponent is odd
        if nn % 2 == 1:
            ans = ans * x
            nn = nn - 1
        # If exponent is even
        else:
            x = x * x
            nn = nn // 2
    # Return reciprocal if original exponent was negative
    return 1.0 / ans if n < 0 else ans

trace.desc: 5 is odd. Multiply ans by 2.0, decrement nn to 4
4 is even. Square x to 4.0, divide nn by 2 to 2
2 is even. Square x to 16.0, divide nn by 2 to 1
1 is odd. Multiply ans by 16.0 to 32.0, decrement nn to 0

Majority Element (> n/2 times).title: Majority Element (> n/2 times)
Majority Element (> n/2 times).problemStatement: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element. The majority element is the element that appears more than ⌊n / 2⌋ times.
edgeCases: All array elements are the same
followUps: Could you solve the problem in linear time and in O(1) space?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use a hash map to count occurrences of each element. Return the element with frequency > n/2.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize an empty dictionary.
2. Iterate through nums, updating frequency counts.
3. If count > n // 2, return the element.
4. Return -1 if not found.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm. The majority element appears > n/2 times, so it will always outvote other elements. We maintain a candidate and its vote count. If count is 0, choose current as candidate. Increment count if element == candidate, else decrement.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize candidate = None, count = 0.
2. Loop through each element in nums.
3. If count == 0, set candidate = element.
4. Increment count if element == candidate, else decrement count.
5. Return candidate.
approaches.code:
def majorityElement(nums):
    # Store candidate majority element
    candidate = None
    # Store vote count
    count = 0
    # Traverse the array
    for num in nums:
        # Update candidate if count is 0
        if count == 0:
            candidate = num
        # Increment vote if match, otherwise decrement
        if num == candidate:
            count += 1
        else:
            count -= 1
    # Return candidate
    return candidate

Majority Element II (> n/3 times).title: Majority Element II (> n/3 times)
Majority Element II (> n/3 times).problemStatement: Given an integer array of size n, find all elements that appear more than ⌊ n/3 ⌋ times.
edgeCases: No element appears more than n/3 times (returns empty list)
followUps: Could you solve the problem in linear time and in O(1) space?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use a hash map to count occurrences of all elements, then filter those with count > n/3.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize a counts dictionary.
2. Iterate and increment counts.
3. Filter counts dictionary to extract elements that exceed len(nums) // 3.
4. Return them.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Extended Boyer-Moore Voting Algorithm. At most two elements can appear more than n/3 times. We keep two candidates and their counts. In the first pass, we identify the top two potential candidates. In the second pass, we verify their actual counts.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Set cand1, cand2 = None, counts = 0.
2. Iterate through nums to update candidates and decrement if mismatching both.
3. Reset actual counts of cand1, cand2 to 0.
4. Recalculate their occurrences.
5. Append to result if they exceed n/3.
6. Return results.

trace.desc: Set cand1 = 1, count1 = 1 since count1 was 0
Set cand2 = 2, count2 = 1 since count2 was 0
Verify counts: count of 1 is 2, count of 2 is 1

Grid Unique Paths.title: Grid Unique Paths
Grid Unique Paths.problemStatement: There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner. The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner. The robot can only move either down or right. Return the number of possible unique paths.
followUps: What if some cells contain obstacles? (Unique Paths II)

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Recursive backtracking. From any cell, the robot can go down or right. The total paths is the sum of paths from down cell and right cell.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Implement countPaths(i, j).
2. If i == m - 1 and j == n - 1, return 1.
3. If i >= m or j >= n, return 0.
4. Return countPaths(i + 1, j) + countPaths(i, j + 1).

approaches.name: Better
approaches.intuition: Dynamic Programming (Tabulation). Create a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents unique paths to reach cell (i, j). Transition: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize dp matrix of size m x n with 1.
2. Iterate i from 1 to m-1, and j from 1 to n-1.
3. dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].
4. Return dp[m-1][n-1].

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Combinatorics. Total steps required = m + n - 2. Down steps = m - 1. Right steps = n - 1. The result is combination (m + n - 2) C (m - 1).
approaches.algorithm:
1. Let N = m + n - 2, r = min(m - 1, n - 1).
2. Calculate combination N C r iteratively.
3. Return result.
approaches.code:
def uniquePaths(m, n):
    # Total number of directions to take
    N = m + n - 2
    # Choose the smaller movement
    r = min(m - 1, n - 1)
    res = 1
    # Compute combination NCr
    for i in range(1, r + 1):
        res = res * (N - r + i) // i
    # Return final combination count
    return res

Reverse Pairs.title: Reverse Pairs
Reverse Pairs.problemStatement: Given an integer array nums, return the number of reverse pairs in the array. A reverse pair is a pair (i, j) where: 0 <= i < j < nums.length and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].
followUps: Can you solve it using a Segment Tree or Fenwick Tree?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use nested loops to inspect all pairs (i, j) where i < j and verify the condition nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize count = 0.
2. Iterate i from 0 to N-1.
3. Iterate j from i+1 to N-1.
4. If nums[i] > 2 * nums[j], count += 1.
5. Return count.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Modified Merge Sort. We count pairs recursively in left and right halves, then count cross pairs where nums[i] > 2 * nums[j] using two pointers, and finally merge the sorted halves.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Implement merge_sort(left, right).
2. Count pairs recursively in (left, mid) and (mid+1, right).
3. Use two pointers i, j to count cross pairs: for each i in left half, advance j in right half while nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. Add (j - (mid + 1)) to count.
4. Merge sorted halves. Return accumulated counts.

trace.desc: Start merge sort with left=0, right=3
Perform count_pairs on sorted left=[4, 6] and right=[1, 2]
i = 0 (val 4). Advance j. nums[0] (4) > 2 * nums[2] (2). Increment j to 3.
Check nums[0] (4) > 2 * nums[3] (4) is False. Add (3 - 2) = 1 to count.
i = 1 (val 6). Advance j. nums[1] (6) > 2 * nums[3] (4). Increment j to 4.
j exceeds boundary. Add (4 - 2) = 2 to count.

Four Sum.title: Four Sum
Four Sum.problemStatement: Given an array nums of n integers and an integer target, return an array of all the unique quadruplets [nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]] such that: 0 <= a, b, c, d < n, a, b, c, and d are distinct, and nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] + nums[d] == target.
edgeCases: Array has less than 4 elements (returns empty list)
followUps: Can you generalize the solution to K-Sum?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Use 4 nested loops to check all quadruplets. Sort each match and add it to a set to remove duplicates.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Run 4 loops: i, j, k, l.
2. If sum is target, sort the quadruplet and insert it as a tuple into set.
3. Convert set of tuples back to list of lists and return.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Sort the array. Fix the first two elements with nested loops (i and j), then use two pointers (left and right) for the remaining two elements to search for matching sum. Skip duplicates to ensure uniqueness.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Sort the array.
2. Loop i from 0 to N-1. If nums[i] == nums[i-1], continue.
3. Loop j from i+1 to N-1. If nums[j] == nums[j-1], continue.
4. Initialize left = j + 1, right = N - 1.
5. Calculate sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right].
6. Adjust pointers and skip duplicate elements appropriately.
7. Return all found quadruplets.

Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.title: Largest Subarray with 0 Sum
Largest Subarray with 0 Sum.problemStatement: Given an array of integers, find the length of the largest subarray with sum equal to 0.
followUps: Can you find the maximum length subarray with sum K?

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: Check all possible subarrays. Compute the sum of each subarray and track the maximum length where sum equals 0.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize max_len = 0.
2. Loop i from 0 to N-1 (start of subarray).
3. Loop j from i to N-1 (end of subarray).
4. Compute subarray sum. If sum == 0, update max_len = max(max_len, j - i + 1).
5. Return max_len.
approaches.code:
def maxLen(arr):
    # Initialize max length of zero-sum subarray
    max_len = 0
    n = len(arr)
    # Check every starting point
    for i in range(n):
        curr_sum = 0
        # Check every ending point
        for j in range(i, n):
            curr_sum += arr[j]
            # Update max length if sum is 0
            if curr_sum == 0:
                max_len = max(max_len, j - i + 1)
    # Return maximum length
    return max_len

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.intuition: Maintain the prefix sum. If the prefix sum has been seen before at index 'prev_idx', it means the elements in between sum to 0. We store the first occurrence of each prefix sum in a hash map.
approaches.algorithm:
1. Initialize sum_map = {}, curr_sum = 0, max_len = 0.
2. Iterate through array. Update curr_sum.
3. If curr_sum == 0, max_len = i + 1.
4. Else, if curr_sum in sum_map, max_len = max(max_len, i - sum_map[curr_sum]).
5. Else, store sum_map[curr_sum] = i.
6. Return max_len.
